messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Peter is a 66-year-old software engineer who has been married for over forty years, but the architecture of his inner life was laid down decades earlier, in a childhood he rarely speaks about. He grew up with a father whose discipline came unpredictably and violently. He remembers one winter evening in particular: he had left a bicycle in the driveway, and his father yanked him inside by the arm, slammed him onto the cold linoleum floor, and beat him with a leather belt. The details that stay with Peter are not the blows themselves but the sensation of the icy floor against his cheek, the smell of stale beer on his father’s breath, and the frantic pounding of his own heart in his ears. That memory still arrives without warning—often when his skin touches a cold surface, or when his heart starts racing from even mild exertion. Each time, his body reacts before his mind has a chance to catch up: his muscles lock, his breath shortens, and he feels an urgent need to scan the room for anything that could be used as a weapon. The startle response has become so ingrained that when a colleague claps him on the shoulder in greeting, Peter jerks away, his pulse already hammering.

These episodes reinforce a conviction that has taken root over a lifetime: people cannot be trusted, and he is permanently an outsider. Peter believes that if he lets his guard down for a moment, danger will find him. Once he had concluded that people could not be trusted, ordinary cues began to feel like warnings—a colleague pausing in the hallway, the unexpected ring of a phone, the jingle of keys in a pocket—each one demanding his eyes dart toward it before his mind could decide whether it mattered. This constant vigilance colors his every interaction. At work, he keeps his desk turned so that he can see the door; in meetings, he notices the sharp corner of a letter opener or the weight of a paperweight. He has come to view his own body as a liability—its reactions betray him, and he avoids paying attention to it whenever possible. When he catches a glimpse of himself in the mirror, he looks away, unsettled by the vulnerability he sees. He has also withdrawn from the small circle of friends he once had, convinced that no one could understand what he carries, and that socializing is simply an invitation to be caught off guard. His wife has learned not to touch him from behind, but even her hand on his arm in the kitchen can trigger a flinch. He does not like the way his body feels under her touch; it reminds him of the cold floor, of being pinned down, of his own helplessness.

Over the years, Peter’s avoidance has deepened the very beliefs it was meant to manage. By steering clear of others, he confirms his sense of being apart. By not looking at his body, he avoids confronting the shame and fragility he associates with it—but the heart still pounds, and the cold still prickles, and each physical sensation becomes another proof that danger is imminent. He has noticed that the more he tries to ignore his bodily signals, the more they intrude. His heart races on a quiet walk; the cold of a glass of water brings the memory crashing back. And each time, the world feels a little more threatening, and he retreats a little further. He is exhausted by the effort of staying on guard. That unrelenting hum of threat made anything with a sharp edge or a sudden sound into a potential signal—the scrape of a chair leg, a car door slamming outside, even the way a coat hung on a hook could catch his attention and hold it until he forced himself to look away. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last month when he found himself staring at a pair of scissors on his desk, his breath shallow, his fists clenched, unable to remember how long he had been frozen there. He is afraid that one day he will not be able to pull himself back, and that the outsider he feels himself to be will become permanently locked inside his own body.
